identity.name: Kingdom of Chiang Mai
native_names: อาณาจักรเชียงใหม่

land.text: Lan Na, the Chiang Mai kingdom under Burmese governors

predecessors.note: The Siamese conquest of 15 January 1775 (infobox) ends Burmese-held Lan Na; the lan-na dossier closes there.

land.text: Burmese-held Chiang Mai and the Lan Na cities

predecessors.note: Chiang Mai was Burmese from August 1763 to January 1775.

land.text: the Chiang Mai kingdom, annexed as Monthon Phayap

successors.note: 'December 1899: Monthon Phayap was established as a full-fledged Monthon to succeed the previous Monthon Lao Chiang'; 'Establishment of Monthon Phayap was formalized in 1900 with Bangkok achieving full control of the north.' The princely title continued to 1939. Cliopatria's Rattanakosin shape takes the north already in 1885 (see notes).

capitals.name: Chiang Mai
capitals.note: Phaya Chaban governor from 1775; 'In 1777, Burmese forces invaded Chiang Mai' and he left the city.

capitals.name: Lampang (Kawila's seat)
capitals.note: Chiang Mai was 'abandoned for twenty years from 1777 to 1797'; Kawila was governor (prince) of Lampang from 1775 and held the north from there (and Pasang). The seat of the Chiang Mai realm in these years is Kawila's Lampang by my reading.

capitals.name: Chiang Mai (Rattana Tingsa Aphinawaburi)
capitals.note: 'Kawila entered Chiang Mai in March 1797' (February 1797 in the Kawila page); he named the new city in 1800; the capital of the Kingdom of Chiang Mai to 1899.

correction.text: the 1775 shape without Chiang Rai, the Burmese-held Chiang Saen country

keyframe_review.note: 1775-1782, 52,465 km2: Chiang Mai, Chiang Rai (97 per cent), Phayao, Mae Hong Son, 42 per cent of Lampang and 23 per cent of Lamphun, with a strip of Myanmar west to the Salween. Chiang Mai was taken from the Burmese on 15 January 1775 and abandoned from 1777; Chiang Rai (Chiang Saen) stayed in Burmese hands: 'Burmese forces of 30,000 men from Burmese-held Chiang Saen' attacked Lampang in 1785 and Chiang Saen fell to the Chiang Mai lords only in 1804. The Cliopatria shape draws the Siamese-held land and the Burmese-held land alike. Correction: without Chiang Rai. Infobox area: none. [Author repair 2026-10-19 after review: the abandonment of the Chiang Mai basin from 1777 to 1797 does not leave this shape: the Chiang Mai page describes an abandoned city, no other state held the land, and the seat is recorded in the capitals strip and as capital_move events (the loss to nobody of 1777 and the gain of 1797 are removed).]

union.text: Bokeo and Louang Namtha, the Mekong and Nam Tha country

correction.text: the Lan Na core without the Burmese-held Chiang Saen country and without the Laotian cells

keyframe_review.note: 1783-1852, 64,890 km2: the 1775 outline plus Bokeo (57 per cent) and Louang Namtha (74 per cent) in Laos, which Cliopatria's Luang Prabang row loses in the same year. No page opened records a Chiang Mai gain there: the Kingdom of Chiang Mai and Kawila pages list the Chiang Saen capture (1804), Kengtung and Mong Hsat (1802) and Mong Yawng (1805), none of them in Laos, and neither page mentions Chiang Khong. Correction for 1783-1803: the 1775 shape without Chiang Rai and without the Laotian cells (they stay with Luang Prabang, whose dossier restores them).

minus.text: Bokeo and Louang Namtha, the Mekong and Nam Tha country

correction.text: the Lan Na core with Chiang Rai after the capture of Chiang Saen in 1804

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1804-1852: Chiang Saen is taken. 'Chiang Mai forces under Thammalangka managed to capture Chiang Saen in 1804' (with Bangkok, Lampang, Nan and Vientiane), and its 23,000 inhabitants were shared among the victors. Chiang Rai joins the realm; the Laotian cells stay out.

minus.text: Bokeo and Louang Namtha, the Mekong and Nam Tha country

correction.text: the 1853 shape without the Laotian cells

keyframe_review.note: 1853-1879, 65,306 km2: the same outline as 1783. Nothing in the page changes the land: Lanna-Siamese forces attacked Kengtung in March 1853 and were repulsed; Mahawong was made King Mahotaraprathet in July 1853; the Chiang Mai treaty with British India was concluded in 1874 and Mae Hong Son founded the same year. The Laotian cells are removed as in 1783.

minus.text: Bokeo and Louang Namtha, the Mekong and Nam Tha country

correction.text: the 1880 shape without the Laotian cells

keyframe_review.note: 1880-1884, 65,306 km2: same outline. The first Siamese commissioner (Kha Luang) was appointed in 1875 and a new one in 1884; the Laotian cells are removed as before.

minus.text: Bokeo and Louang Namtha, the Mekong and Nam Tha country

correction.text: the 1880 shape (without the Laotian cells) held to December 1899 as a Siamese tributary

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1885-1899: the kingdom continues until Monthon Phayap in December 1899 as a tributary under Siamese commissioners ('Tributes to Bangkok were sent triennially'; Phraya Kraikosa ordered in 1892 'to cede Thirteen Shan and Karenni Towns of the Trans-Salween area to British Burma'). Cliopatria ends the row in 1884 and draws the north as Rattanakosin land from 1885 (Chiang Mai 99 per cent); the page does not support an annexation before 1899.

ledger.note: 15 January 1775: the Siamese take Chiang Mai from the Burmese. Taksin 'marched his army north to attack Burmese-held Chiang Mai' in December 1774; generals Chakri and Surasi, with Kawila of Lampang, took it; infobox 'Siamese conquest 15 January 1775'; Phaya Chaban was made governor of Chiang Mai and Kawila of Lampang (Chiang Mai page).

region.text: Chiang Mai, Lamphun, Lampang, Phayao and Mae Hong Son, without Chiang Saen

ledger.note: January 1775: Lan Na passes from Burma to Chiang Mai and Thonburi. 'The Siamese were able to take Chiang Mai in January 1775' (Burmese-Siamese War 1775-1776 page); 'Lanna came under Thonburi tributary'.

1777: Chiang Mai is abandoned and the realm is held from Kawila's Lampang. 'Due to Burmese military pressure, Chiang Mai was abandoned for twenty years from 1777 to 1797' (Kingdom of Chiang Mai page, reopened); Kawila 'established himself temporarily at Pasang' and 'Lampang remained the main city in Kawila's dominions'; the Thonburi page: 'In 1777, Burmese forces invaded Chiang Mai' and Phaya Chaban left. The page describes an abandoned city, not land that left the realm and that no other state took, so the basin stays in the keyframes and no loss is recorded. Lampang as the seat is my reading (confidence 2). [Replaces the 1777 loss of the basin to nobody, removed after review.]

1785: the Burmese besiege Lampang. 'Burmese forces of 30,000 men from Burmese-held Chiang Saen' laid siege to Lampang in the Nine Armies' War; Kawila held out for four months; again in January 1786 and in 1788 ('45,000 men attacked Lampang and Pasang').

region.text: the Burmese are beaten at Lampang and Pasang

ledger.note: March 1788: the Burmese are beaten at Lampang and Pasang. 'The Burmese were defeated at Lampang and Pasang in March 1788' (Kawila page).
1797: Bodawpaya sends the Burmese again. The Burmese 'sent forces of 55,000 men to attack Chiang Mai in 1797' (Kawila page: through Mongnai and Mong Pan).

March 1797: Kawila re-enters Chiang Mai and the seat returns. 'Kawila entered Chiang Mai in March 1797' (the Kawila page has February 1797); Chiang Mai 'was finally restored as political and cultural center of Lanna in 1797', after Kawila took 'a portion of population from Lampang to restore Chiang Mai' in 1796. The Burmese attacked the city in 1797 (contest events). [Replaces the 1797 gain of the basin from nobody, removed after review.]
April 1798: the Burmese are repelled. 'The Burmese were soundly defeated and repelled in April 1798' (Kawila page); a second Burmese attack in 1802 was repelled by Siamese relief forces.

1802: Kengtung falls to Chiang Mai. Thammalangka 'proceeded to capture Kengtung or Chiang Tung, which had been under Burmese suzerainty, in 1802'; Kawila sent him 'to seize Mong Hsat in 1802' and Chom Hong, Bodawpaya's governor, was captured (Kawila page). Kengtung is outside Cliopatria's shape; the page speaks of capture, which I read as a short-lived subjection.

December 1802: Kawila becomes tributary king of Chiang Mai. 'In December 1802, in recognition of Kawila's contribution in defense of the north against Burma' Rama I appointed him (infobox: installation of Kawila December 1802; the Kawila page also has 14 September 1802). The princely house of Kawila rules Chiang Mai from here.

region.text: Chiang Saen and the Chiang Rai country

ledger.note: 1804: Chiang Saen is taken from the Burmese. 'In 1804, combined allied forces from Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Lampang, Nan and Vientiane attacked Chiang Saen'; 'Chiang Mai forces under Thammalangka managed to capture Chiang Saen in 1804'; its 23,000 inhabitants were divided in five portions.
1813: Kengtung returns to Burma. 'Maha Hkanan eventually decided to accept Burmese suzerainty in 1813' after Thammalangka's Lanna force supporting him was beaten by the Burmese in 1808.

July 1853: Mahawong is appointed King Mahotaraprathet of Chiang Mai after King Mongkut raised the Lanna lords from Phraya to Chao in 1853. The Chiang Mai and Siamese attack on Kengtung of March 1853 was repulsed.

1892: the Trans-Salween towns go to British Burma. Phraya Kraikosa was ordered in 1892 'to cede Thirteen Shan and Karenni Towns of the Trans-Salween area to British Burma'. These lands lie beyond Cliopatria's 1783 outline; the region is my reading of 'Shan and Karenni' (Kayah).

December 1899: Chiang Mai is annexed as Monthon Phayap. 'December 1899: Monthon Phayap was established as a full-fledged Monthon to succeed the previous Monthon Lao Chiang'; Songsuradet was recalled in 1899; the ceremonial title ended with Prince Kaew's death on 3 June 1939.

wars.name: Siamese conquest of Chiang Mai (1774-1775)
wars.outcome: Chiang Mai taken on 15 January 1775; Lan Na became a Thonburi tributary; the Burmese counterattack from Chiang Saen of September 1775 failed.
wars.note: The Burmese-Siamese War 1775-1776 page: 'Nemyo Thihapate and Thado Mindin took off from Chiang Saen to invade Chiang Mai in September 1775.'

wars.name: Burmese sieges of Lampang (Nine Armies' War)
wars.outcome: Kawila held Lampang against 30,000 Burmese in 1785-1786 and 45,000 in 1788; the Burmese were beaten at Lampang and Pasang in March 1788.
wars.note: The Burmese came from Burmese-held Chiang Saen.

wars.name: Burmese invasions of Chiang Mai (1797-1798, 1802)
wars.outcome: Repelled in April 1798 and again in 1802 by Siamese relief forces; Bodawpaya had set up Chom Hong at Mong Hsat in 1802 as a rival.

wars.name: Capture of Chiang Saen
wars.outcome: Chiang Saen taken in 1804 by combined forces from Bangkok, Chiang Mai, Lampang, Nan and Vientiane; Anouvong of Vientiane took part.

wars.name: Chiang Mai campaigns against Kengtung
wars.outcome: Kengtung captured in 1802 and Mong Yawng in 1805; Lanna forces beaten in 1808; Maha Hkanan accepted Burmese suzerainty in 1813; the attacks of 1850 and March 1853 failed.

certainty.note: No treaty line: the frontiers with Burma (Salween, Kengtung), Nan, Phrae and Luang Prabang are approximate. The Trans-Salween frontier was fixed with Britain in 1892-1894, but the lines are not on the pages opened.

notes:
Page budget 5; four pages opened (WebFetch summaries, so every quotation is the summariser's quotation). No infobox area, so the comparison with Cliopatria's 52,000-65,000 km2 could not be made.

Cliopatria's row: (1) it runs to 1884, but the page keeps the kingdom as a tributary to December 1899 (Monthon Phayap), so the end is 1899 and a new keyframe covers 1885-1899; Cliopatria's Rattanakosin shape takes the north (Chiang Mai 99 per cent) from 1885, so rattanakosin-kingdom's 1885-1899 shape should show it as a vassal, not as direct land, or this dossier should be cut back to 1884 by the reviewer; (2) the 1775 and 1783 shapes include Chiang Rai (Chiang Saen), which was Burmese until 1804; (3) the 1783 expansion into Bokeo and Louang Namtha (Laos) is not supported by any page and duplicates the Luang Prabang loss of the same year (corrected in both dossiers); (4) Lampang and Lamphun are split between this row (42 and 23 per cent) and the Siamese rows (58 and 77 per cent): left as drawn.

Chiang Mai itself was abandoned 1777-1797 on the page; the realm ran from Kawila's Lampang and Pasang. The Siamese suzerainty (vassal tint) belongs to the thonburi-kingdom ledger (from January 1775) and the rattanakosin-kingdom dossier. Pages disagree: Kawila entered Chiang Mai in February 1797 (Kawila page) or March 1797 (Chiang Mai page); Kawila's reign 1782-1815/1816 on the Chiang Mai page and 1802-1813 in its infobox; his consecration 14 September or December 1802; Lamphun became a princedom in 1805, 1806, 1814 or 1819.

Not written: the ruler strip (the pages give Kawila 1782/1802-1816, Mahawong from 1853, Kawilorot from 1856, Inthawichayanon 1873-1897, Inthawarorot 1901-1910, Kaew Nawarat 1910-1939, but not Thammalangka's successors or the 1870-1873 gap in a form I could check); Nan and Phrae (their own dynasties, no Cliopatria row). Counterparts needing dossiers: kengtung (Burmese-suzerain Shan state), nan, phrae, lamphun (princely seat 1805-1814).

Repair after review (2026-10-19). (1) The 1777 loss of the Chiang Mai basin to nobody and the 1797 gain from nobody are removed, as the review preferred: the Kingdom of Chiang Mai page (reopened) says 'Chiang Mai was abandoned for twenty years from 1777 to 1797' and that Kawila 'established himself temporarily at Pasang' while 'Lampang remained the main city', i.e. an abandoned city, not land that left the realm; no keyframe ever dropped the basin, so the loss and gain contradicted the shapes. The abandonment now stands as two capital_move events (1777 to Lampang, March 1797 back to Chiang Mai) and in the capitals strip. (2) End year 1899 against Cliopatria's Rattanakosin shapes, which draw Chiang Mai from 1885: no change by me; for the orchestrator and the author of rattanakosin-kingdom (se-01-j), whose 1885-1898 keyframes should drop the Chiang Mai cells and show the north as a vassal tint, or this dossier must be cut back to 1884. (3) The 1804 gain of Chiang Rai now has its mirror: a 1804 loss in the konbaung-dynasty ledger; Konbaung's keyframes hold Chiang Rai from 1775 to 1803. The Lampang and Lamphun cells that Cliopatria gives to the Thonburi shape (58 and 77 per cent) are now a January 1775 gain in the thonburi-kingdom ledger, with a matching loss in konbaung-dynasty's. The ruler strip is still not written (a gap for the gap-filler; page to try: Chiang Mai monarchs).
